name: PT Metro Healthcare Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Metro Healthcare: a real hospital turnaround inside a price that assumes a much bigger one
frontmatter.summary: Metro Healthcare has genuinely turned its hospitals around this year: revenue, operating profit and cash generation all inflected. But the shares capitalise that turnaround at a multiple that requires the step-change to repeat every year for a decade. Our DCF, cross-checked against hospital peers, values the equity far below the market price. SELL.
thesis: The hospital business inflected in 2026: nine-month revenue rose on volume and tariff while operating expenses grew far more slowly, taking operating profit to a level the company has never earned on a full-year basis [S5].

The FY2025 profit was not an operating profit: investment income inside revenue, carrying no cost of sales, produced most of the gross profit [S4]. Strip it out and the hospitals lost money at the operating line that year.
The balance sheet has been rebuilt around sukuk and bank debt: gross debt rose again in 2026 while cash sits idle, so financial expenses now absorb almost all of operating profit [S4][S5].

At the current price the market pays a multiple of sales and EBITDA that no hospital operator in this market sustains; our DCF needs FY2027E growth of 38.8% to justify the price, against our base case of 8.7% [S0].

The free float is a third of the shares and ownership is concentrated but compliant: insiders hold 49.9% and the accounts show no second controlling vehicle [S0][S4]. The stock trades on a thin institutional base, which is where a valuation can detach from cash flow.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: the first full year that tests whether the 2026 revenue step-up was volume or tariff
Sukuk refinancing window: a large slice of the sukuk issued in 2026 matures or reprices within twelve months of the year-end accounts
Sukuk Ijarah Phase II: the second half of the shelf programme is still unissued and the first series comes due within twelve months of the year-end accounts
Conversion of advances for property and equipment into operating beds at the hospital under construction

blocks.text: We initiate Metro Healthcare Indonesia at **SELL** with a target price of **Rp34**, -90.5% against the Rp356 close on 13 November 2026. The company operates a chain of private hospitals in Greater Jakarta, Banten and East Java and has just produced the best operating result in its listed history: operating profit of 77.2 IDR bn for the first nine months of 2026 on revenue of 367 IDR bn, with positive operating cash flow after years of losses [S5]. That improvement is real and it is the core of the bull case. Our problem is not with the business; it is with the price.

The market is capitalising the turnaround as if it were the start of a decade of compounding. At Rp356 the equity is worth several times the entire invested capital of the group, and the enterprise value is a very large multiple of the EBITDA the business will earn this year even if the recent run-rate holds [S0]. Our primary method, a ten-year discounted cash flow at a cost of capital of 11.0%, values the equity at Rp32 a share. It carries a weight of 60.0%, with the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 30.0% and P/E at 10.0% [S0]. Both cross-checks are struck on trailing FY2025 metrics that this name makes unrepresentative — the EV/EBITDA result lands close to the DCF, while the P/E result is -90.4% versus it because trailing profit is almost entirely one-off investment income — and we test the blend against book value in the valuation section; even the trading multiples that the market itself applies give nothing close to today's price [S0].

What the market is paying for, in our reading, is a story rather than a cash-flow stream it can see in the accounts. The 2026 revenue jump is genuine but its cause is not disclosed in a way that lets us extrapolate it: the company's own revenue disaggregation shows hospital services rising sharply while a separate line, investment income, contributed a large block of zero-cost revenue in FY2025 and a smaller but still material block in the first nine months of 2026 [S4][S5]. Our base case assumes the hospital business keeps growing at a rate well above nominal GDP for five years, holds the improved cost ratio flat, and reinvests at a normal hospital build cycle. Even then the equity is worth a fraction of today's price.

The variant view, stated plainly: we think the market is treating a closely held small cap as a platform. Insiders hold 49.9% of the shares, a single foreign nominee holds 17.4%, and the public float is 32.2% [S0][S4]. A price built on a third of the capital changing hands, with no disclosed institutional anchor, is exactly where we would expect a valuation to detach from cash flow. We make no claim about index eligibility either way; the ownership facts alone explain why the marginal buyer is retail.

What moves the value, in order of importance: the durability of the 2026 hospital revenue step-up (if it holds for four more quarters our bull case applies); the cost of the sukuk and bank debt, because financial expenses currently consume nearly all of operating profit [S5]; and the timing of the next hospital, because the company has already paid 367 IDR bn of advances for property and equipment that have not yet produced a single rupiah of revenue [S5].

Metro Healthcare Indonesia owns and operates private hospitals under the Metro Hospital brand. The company was established in 2015 with the acquisition of a maternity and children's hospital in Tangerang and listed in 2020; it now manages 7.0 count hospitals in Tangerang, Jakarta, Cikarang, Cikupa, Mojosari and Sidoarjo [S3]. The corporate structure is a holding company over operating subsidiaries, each of which holds a hospital licence; the consolidated group includes entities for hospital operations, trading of medical devices and laboratory equipment, and property [S4]. Employees numbered 848 people at the end of September 2026, down slightly from the prior year-end [S5].

The operating model is a mid-market private hospital network that accepts both insured and self-pay patients. The company's own description of its competitive advantage is explicit: it positions hospitals in growing regional catchments rather than in the saturated centre of Jakarta, accepts insured patients from both corporate and government payers, and adds bed capacity in every hospital it acquires or builds [S6]. Its service range runs from outpatient polyclinics through intensive care to Class III and Super VIP inpatient rooms, which lets it serve both the national health insurance book and the private segment from the same facility [S6].

Patient volumes give the scale of the operation. In 2024 the group served 269,763 patients outpatients and 41,441 patients inpatients [S6]. Those numbers matter because they set the operating leverage: a hospital carries doctors, nurses and equipment against a fixed cost base, so incremental patients drop through at high margin once the beds are staffed. That is the mechanism behind the 2026 result, and it is the reason the rest of this report spends so much time on whether the volume gain persists.

Revenue splits two ways. Hospital services produced 342 IDR bn of the FY2025 total, and a second segment, investment income, produced 97.8 IDR bn with no cost of sales at all [S4]. Within hospital services the disclosed disaggregation separates inpatient and outpatient revenue and, inside each, drugs and medical supplies, medical services, medical support services, emergency services and administration income [S4]. The largest single cost is medical professional fees, followed by the claim-tariff difference with the national insurer, then medicines and supplies, then depreciation [S4].

The strategy is set out in the annual report as a combination of bed additions, outpatient strengthening and preparation for the government's standard inpatient class regulation, which requires hospitals to move toward uniform room classes [S6]. Management also describes a training centre for health workers and a patient-facing application as adjacent projects [S3]. In practice the capital programme is the strategy: cash has gone out the door as advance payments for property and equipment rather than as completed assets, and the group's growth in any year is largely a function of when those advances turn into beds [S4][S5].

The controlling shareholder and the board are described in the final section. The relevant point for the business model is that the company is closely held, with insiders holding roughly half the shares and a free float that the registry puts at a minority of the capital [S0]. There is no second listed vehicle in the group and no material related-party revenue: the accounts state that there were no sales or service revenues to related parties in either FY2025 or FY2024 [S4].

Indonesian private hospitals sit between two payers: the national health insurance scheme, which pays administered tariffs and dominates volume, and private insurance and self-pay, which pay market rates and dominate margin. A hospital's profitability therefore depends less on medical skill than on payer mix, occupancy and the ability to negotiate with the national insurer. The sector's structural constraint is that bed capacity is licensed and takes years to build, so supply responds slowly to demand, and the constraint on growth is capital and licensing rather than demand.

Demand for private hospital care in Indonesia grows with population, urbanisation and the expansion of health insurance coverage. The company's annual report describes the national healthcare sector as resilient, cites the national insurer's reform programme and rising public awareness of quality medical services, and points to government support for the standard inpatient class regulation as factors that expand access [S6]. That is the company's own framing, but the direction is consistent with what the accounts show: hospital revenue grew from 319 IDR bn in FY2024 to 334 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 alone, within a FY2025 total of 440 IDR bn, of which hospital services were 342 IDR bn and 97.8 IDR bn was investment income [S4][S5]. Whatever the mix of volume and tariff, the addressable market has been expanding fast enough to support that.

The competitive landscape is a tiered one. At the top sit the large national networks with dozens of hospitals and city-wide brands; below them a long tail of single-site and small-chain operators; and in between, regional groups such as Metro that own a handful of facilities in contiguous catchments. Metro is a challenger, not a leader: 7.0 count hospitals against national networks an order of magnitude larger. Its differentiation is geographic — secondary cities and the edges of Greater Jakarta where the large networks are thinner — and payer breadth, since it accepts both the national insurer and corporate schemes [S6].

The moat is thin but not absent. Hospital competition is local: a patient will travel a limited distance for elective care, so a hospital with the only intensive care unit in a district has real pricing and referral power regardless of its brand. Metro's hospitals in Cikupa, Cikarang, Mojosari and Sidoarjo fit that pattern. What it lacks is the brand and doctor network that let a national chain recruit specialists and fill beds faster; its own annual report lists doctor recruitment and retention as a principal risk, alongside competition and the availability of medical personnel [S6]. We would not underwrite a widening moat. We underwrite a regional operator that earns a normal return on invested capital once its beds mature.

Five forces, briefly. Buyer power is high and rising: the national insurer sets tariffs administratively, and the accounts show the cost of the gap between billed and reimbursed claims — the claim-tariff difference — rising from a large line in FY2025 to a much larger one in the first nine months of 2026 [S4][S5]. Supplier power is moderate: medical devices and drugs are imported and priced in dollars, so a weak rupiah raises input costs, and the macro desk has the currency under balance-of-payments pressure. Threat of new entrants is constrained by licensing and capital but not eliminated: the government's own policy is to expand capacity. Substitute products are limited for acute care and strong for diagnostics, which is why outpatient and laboratory services are contested. Rivalry is local and intensifying as national chains move into secondary cities.

Regulation is the dominant external influence. The standard inpatient class regulation changes the physical configuration of wards; the national insurer's tariff policy sets the ceiling on the largest payer; and the health ministry's licensing rules govern expansion. The company's annual report treats all three as strategic variables rather than background [S6]. For an investor the practical consequence is that revenue per patient is partly an administrative decision, which caps how much of a demand upturn a hospital can keep.

The national health insurer pays hospitals on a case-mix basis: a fixed tariff per diagnosis group rather than per item of care. Hospitals that treat a case more cheaply than the tariff keep the difference; hospitals that treat it more expensively absorb the loss. Tariffs are revised periodically after negotiation between the government, the insurer and provider associations, and each revision resets the economics of the entire hospital sector at once. This is why hospital earnings in Indonesia move in steps rather than smoothly, and why a single year's revenue jump cannot be extrapolated without knowing which side of a tariff revision it came from.

The five-year record is one of a capital-intensive build followed by a sharp operating inflection. Revenue rose from IDR260.4bn in FY2022 to IDR439.8bn in FY2025 while the group ran operating losses in each of the first three years, turning a small operating profit only in FY2025 [S0][S4]. The reported profit in FY2025, 5.1 IDR bn, was not earned by the hospitals: investment income of 97.8 IDR bn sat inside revenue with no matching cost of sales, so the hospital business itself produced an operating loss once that line is removed [S4]. Our restated history shows the same thing from the other direction: FY2025 EBITDA of IDR96.3bn is the first positive full-year figure in the series [S0].

The cost structure explains both the losses and the turnaround. Cost of revenue was 225 IDR bn in FY2025 against 214 IDR bn in FY2024, with the largest components medical professional fees, the claim-tariff difference with the national insurer, medicines and supplies, and depreciation [S4]. Depreciation is charged entirely to cost of revenue and is disclosed only in the notes: 26.3 IDR bn in FY2025 and 25.5 IDR bn in FY2024 [S4]. The data pack carries no depreciation line at all, which is why we restate it from the accounts; without it the EBITDA and cash-flow history in any pack-based model is meaningless for a company with IDR96.3bn of EBITDA against a property portfolio of this size.

Operating expenses were IDR145.1bn in FY2025, or roughly a third of revenue [S4]. That FY2025 ratio is not the run-rate. Nine-month 2025 operating expenses were 88.8 IDR bn against a full-year IDR145.1bn, so a disproportionate share of the year's cost was booked in the final quarter, and it sits in salaries and allowances: 92.7 IDR bn for the full year against 53.9 IDR bn in the nine months, while headcount fell from 848 people to a lower figure in 2026 [S4][S5]. That is a year-end compensation true-up, not a cost level. In the first nine months of 2026 operating expenses were 96.5 IDR bn, or 24.9% of the revenue we forecast for the full year, and they grew only single digits on the prior-year period [S5]. We build the forecast year as nine months of actual plus one quarter at that run-rate, 24.9% of revenue, and hold it flat: the group employs 848 people people and the base case does not fund a new hospital's worth of staffing before the beds exist.

The revenue build for our forecast is calendar 2026, not the trailing twelve months the pack shows. FY2026E is the nine-month actual of 367 IDR bn, which already includes 32.6 IDR bn of investment income, plus a fourth quarter built as Q4-2025 hospital revenue grown at the rate hospital services actually grew in the first nine months; that gives IDR518.0bn, 17.8% above FY2025A [S5][S4]. The LTM of the pack counts Q4-2025 instead, a quarter that carried 97.8 IDR bn of investment income the nine-month comparative shows as nil, so it cannot be the base for a forward margin. We treat the 32.6 IDR bn already earned as the last of that income: the policy note defines the line as interest plus realised and unrealised trading gains on a time-deposit book, not a portfolio yield, so no further gain is forecast [S4]. Reported revenue therefore grows 8.7% in FY2027E as that non-recurring line drops out even though hospital revenue grows at the rate we assume, then fades to 13.0%, 11.0% and 9.0% on the seven-hospital base.

The hospital margin needs an honest restatement, because the annual comparison misleads. On a like-for-like basis the hospital gross margin fell, not rose: comparing nine months with nine months, the margin narrowed by several points, and the whole of the fall is one line. The claim-tariff difference with the national insurer rose from 23.2 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2025 to 82.2 IDR bn in the same period of 2026, which against hospital revenue of 334 IDR bn is now a quarter of the top line [S5]. Every other cost line grew at roughly half the rate of hospital revenue: medical professional fees, drugs and supplies, support services and depreciation all lagged [S5]. Ex that single line the hospital margin improved, which is why operating profit doubled.

We hold the last actual. The forecast carries the 46.4% blended margin of calendar 2026, of which 32.6 IDR bn of zero-cost investment income is a large part, and from FY2027E the blended margin drops to the hospital level of 43.4% because that income does not recur [S4][S5]. The claim-tariff difference is the swing factor and nobody has explained it: 58.0 IDR bn for the whole of FY2025, and already 82.2 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S4][S5]. If the latest period is a settlement true-up the margin we forecast is too low and the bull case applies; if it is the new reimbursement relationship it is permanent. The accounts do not say which, so the base case holds the observed level rather than improving it.

Cash flow is the part of the story the market seems to ignore. Operating cash flow turned positive in FY2025 and stayed positive in the first nine months of 2026 [S0][S5]. Capital expenditure, however, is not what the cash-flow statement's plant-and-equipment line suggests: the group pays for construction as advances to contractors, and the relevant figure is the 367 IDR bn of advances outstanding at September 2026, which is cash already gone that has not yet become a depreciating asset [S5]. Free cash flow was therefore negative through the build and turns positive only as the build completes. Our forecast puts capex at 4.0% of revenue in FY2026E, because the cash is already spent, rebuilding to 8.0% as the next phase starts.

The balance sheet is levered in a way the equity market does not seem to price. Interest-bearing debt was IDR1,083.6bn at the end of FY2025 and IDR1,551.4bn at 30 September 2026, after the group issued a new Sukuk Ijarah series under a shelf programme and used part of the proceeds to repay the maturing Wakalah series [S4][S5]. The components matter: two Ijarah series with coupons disclosed at the mid-sevens and high-eights, the remaining Wakalah at double digits, and bank and multifinance facilities at a similar cost to the weighted average [S5][S4]. Cash at the same date was 900 IDR bn plus 61.5 IDR bn of time deposits, so net debt of that balance sheet is a far smaller number than gross debt — but the cash is not free: financial expenses of 80.4 IDR bn in FY2025 and a higher run-rate in 2026 consume nearly all of operating profit [S4][S5]. The model's FY2026E year-end line shows net debt of IDR585.0bn because it rolls the September actual through the fourth quarter's forecast cash flow; the valuation bridge uses the September net debt itself. A company that borrows at those coupons and leaves the uncommitted proceeds in current accounts earning next to nothing is either pre-funding a specific asset or destroying value; the use-of-proceeds note commits only the refinancing tranche, and we treat the rest as a risk rather than a benefit.

Working capital is negative, which helps. Trade payables and accrued expenses exceed receivables and inventory, so growth in revenue releases cash rather than absorbing it — the operating working capital position was a small negative number at September 2026 [S0]. That is typical of hospital operations, where patients pay at the point of service and suppliers are paid on terms.

On earnings quality we run the house screens. The accruals ratio is not a flag: net profit has tracked or trailed operating cash flow in each of the last three years, and the FY2025 profit was backed by operating cash flow larger than the profit itself [S0]. The divergence flags are more interesting. Revenue grew far faster than receivables in 2026, which is the healthy direction; the item that would normally be a warning — a large non-operating income line flattering profit — is present, but it is disclosed as a separate revenue segment rather than buried [S4]. The classification is aggressive in presentation terms, not fraudulent: a zero-cost investment gain inside revenue inflates the revenue base and the gross margin, and any model that takes those at face value will overvalue the company. We have restated around it in the analysis above even though the engine keeps the reported revenue line.

The genuine earnings-quality flag is governance of disclosure rather than of cash. The company reports a claim-tariff difference that moves by tens of billions between periods without a note explaining the driver; it holds a trillion rupiah of new sukuk proceeds in cash without disclosing the intended use in the interim accounts; and its investment income arrives in round numbers that suggest a small number of discrete transactions rather than a portfolio yield [S4][S5]. None of these is manipulation-class on the evidence we have. All of them are reasons to demand a wider discount than a clean operator would command.

We value Metro Healthcare on a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method, cross-checked against the EV/EBITDA and P/E multiples that hospital investors actually transact on. The reasons are structural. A hospital group's value is dominated by assets that are not yet earning: beds under construction, advances to contractors, licences and land. A current-year earnings multiple cannot see those, and this company's current-year earnings are distorted by an investment-income line and a capital structure that has just been rebuilt. The DCF can carry the build-out, the leverage and the tax shield explicitly.

The cost of capital comes from the house macro deck and the hospitals method card, not from a judgement call on the day. The risk-free rate is 7.4%; for a rupiah asset the engine first deducts the Indonesia sovereign default spread of 1.6%, so the rate applied to beta is the net figure rather than the gross sovereign yield. The mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, and the unlevered beta 0.77, levered to 0.85 at the group's market debt-to-equity of 13.1%. That produces a cost of equity of 11.5%. Debt costs 9.4% before tax, the realised rate across the sukuk and bank facilities, and at weights of 88.4% equity and 11.6% debt the weighted average cost of capital is 11.0% [S0].

The beta is the one input we set rather than observe, and we say so. The house universe carries no regression for CARE or for its closest listed peers, and an industry beta default produces a cost of equity and a weighted average cost of capital below the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent for rupiah assets. Rather than publish an out-of-band discount rate for a stock that has halved over the past year and carries a leveraged, capital-intensive balance sheet, we set the unlevered beta at 0.77, which places the WACC at the floor of the band at 11.0% with a cost of equity of 11.5%. The beta is calibrated from the band, not from a regression, and the sensitivity table shows what a higher cost of capital would do: the value falls further, so the direction of the call does not depend on this choice.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,290.1bn and an equity value of Rp32 per share, with 58.6% of the value in the terminal period. That is a high terminal share and it deserves an argument rather than an apology. Two things hold it: the explicit period is ten years and every year of it is fully charged for capex and working capital, and the terminal free cash flow grows at 5.0%, below the explicit-period rate and below nominal GDP. The multiple-survival test is the sharper check. The terminal value discounts back to a modest EBITDA multiple on the IDR230.8bn the business earns then; the price today capitalises the IDR138.5bn of FY2026E EBITDA at 89.7x, which is the entry multiple. Paying an entry multiple many times the exit multiple is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and the method card names that as the dominant failure mode for premium-multiple names in this market. The life of the model is ten years because that is the length of a hospital build cycle for a company this size; a longer horizon would add years of hospitals the balance sheet cannot currently fund.

The engine's two multiple cross-checks are computed on trailing FY2025 metrics, and that is how we report them: neither is re-based onto a forecast year. Trailing EBITDA of IDR96.3bn contains 97.8 IDR bn of zero-cost investment income, so the hospital business was close to break-even at the operating line that year, and trailing parent profit of 5.1 IDR bn is almost entirely the same income. On that trailing EBITDA the peer-median EV/EBITDA gives Rp29 a share, -9.0% versus the DCF. It lands close to the DCF for a compensating reason rather than a causal one: the multiple capitalises income the DCF excludes, while the valuation bridge deducts the investment book that generates it, so the two effects broadly offset and the cross-check corroborates the order of magnitude, not the growth path. The P/E rule on trailing parent profit gives Rp3, -90.4% versus the DCF, because that profit is almost entirely investment income; it stays in the table as a disclosure at a 10.0% weight and is not averaged into the target. We weight the DCF at 60.0% and the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 30.0%, and report the table as it stands rather than substituting a forward strike the engine does not compute.

The asset test is the one this valuation has to pass before it is published, because a DCF can discount a real business into a number that no asset owner would accept. On our FY2026E balance sheet net property, plant and equipment is IDR3,652.8bn against a DCF enterprise value of IDR1,290.1bn, and our target sits below the book value per share of Rp91. A replacement-cost or P/B floor fails here for the same reason it fails for every Indonesian hospital built in the last decade: what a hospital costs to build and what it earns are set by different people, and the claim-tariff line is now a large and rising share of hospital revenue. A network earning a mid-single-digit return on a fixed-asset base this large, against a 11.0% cost of capital, is worth less than the money sunk into it; replacement cost only sets a floor for a new entrant that can earn its cost of capital on a new build, and the evidence is that this one cannot. We therefore use book value as corroboration rather than as a method, and we state the implied exit explicitly: the terminal value is 58.6% of enterprise value, so on the IDR230.8bn of FY2035E EBITDA it discounts back to an exit multiple well below the 89.7x the market pays for FY2026E EBITDA today. An exit below entry is the direction a DCF must run for a capital-intensive operator; the reverse would be multiple expansion in disguise.

The 367 IDR bn of advances for property and equipment is treated as an asset already paid for. It is carried in the valuation bridge at its sunk cost, which is what it is — cash out of the door for beds that do not yet earn — and the base case does not also forecast the revenue those beds will produce. The bridge and the forecast therefore do not double-count: the bridge credits the cash already spent, the DCF earns a return only on what is operating today, and once the beds open the revenue appears in the forecast and the bridge item comes out.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest way to state what the price believes. Holding our cost of capital, our margins, our capex and our terminal growth, the current price requires FY2027E revenue growth of 38.8% — more than four times our base case of 8.7%, and roughly the 2026 step-up repeated without any fade. That is not a forecast anyone has published; it is what the arithmetic demands. A buyer of the shares at Rp356 is therefore underwriting not a turnaround but a permanently higher growth regime, and the accounts do not yet show one.

The multiple-survival test makes the same point from the other side. Our DCF implies an exit enterprise value at the end of the explicit period that is a modest multiple of the EBITDA it earns then; today's price implies an entry multiple several times that. Buying at a higher multiple than the business will exit on is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and the method card is explicit that this is the dominant failure mode for premium-multiple names in this market.

Scenarios widen the range but do not change the sign. Our bear case values the shares at Rp20, the base case at Rp32 and the bull case at Rp52, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% [S0]. Even the bull case, which assumes the 2026 growth rate repeats for years and margins expand, values the equity far below today's price. That asymmetry is the finding.

The risks that matter for this call are, in order: that the 2026 revenue step-up is not repeatable; that the government's reimbursement policy squeezes the margin permanently; that the new debt is more expensive than we assume; that the capital programme consumes more cash than we forecast; and that our own valuation is too harsh on a company we may be misreading.

**Regulatory (high likelihood, high impact).** The national insurer sets the tariff and the government sets the ward configuration. The claim-tariff difference line in the accounts is the visible cost of that relationship, and it more than trebled year on year in the first nine months of 2026 [S5]. A further tightening would hit gross margin directly and there is no offsetting pricing power.

**Macro and currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Medical devices and drugs are imported; the macro desk has the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure with the currency expected to stay weak. A weaker rupiah raises input costs that the national insurer does not reimburse. Higher domestic rates also raise the cost of the sukuk at each refinancing.

**Operational (medium likelihood, high impact).** The 2026 result came from a cost base that did not grow with revenue. Hospital operations do not work that way for long: staffing must follow occupancy, and a new hospital adds fixed costs before it adds patients. The 367 IDR bn of advances outstanding has to convert into beds that earn, and the company has not disclosed the opening date or the expected ramp [S5].

**Liquidity and leverage (medium likelihood, high impact).** Gross debt of IDR1,551.4bn at the September 2026 balance sheet with a large sukuk component creates a refinancing wall. The group issued a trillion rupiah and repaid half within the same nine months, which suggests it is managing maturities actively; it also means the interest burden is now a fixed claim ahead of equity [S5].

**Governance and liquidity (high likelihood, low impact on value, high impact on price).** Ownership is concentrated enough that the free float is a minority of the shares, so the marginal buyer is retail rather than institutional [S0][S4]. That cuts both ways: it is part of why the price can detach from value, and a future free-float expansion would broaden the buyer base.

**Risk to our call (medium likelihood, high impact).** We could be wrong if the group is about to acquire a hospital with the cash it raised. A value-accretive acquisition would add EBITDA we have not forecast, and the market may be pricing exactly that. We searched for such an announcement and found none [S3][S5][S8]; until one is disclosed it cannot be in a most-likely base case. If it appears, the estimates change and so will the rating.

The bear case assumes the 2026 step-up is a tariff and settlement effect rather than durable volume: growth decelerates six percentage points below base, the claim-tariff shortfall keeps gross margin two points lower, and the fixed cost base is under-absorbed. The bull case assumes the opposite with mirrored magnitudes: growth six points above base, gross margin two points higher as tariff revisions catch up, and the cost ratio improving as new beds fill. We deliberately keep the shocks symmetric and confined to the same three drivers in both directions; an asymmetric bear would be a prediction about our own discomfort rather than about the business.

The signposts that would change our view, in order: two more quarters of hospital revenue growth at or above the 2026 run-rate without a matching rise in the claim-tariff difference; a disclosed acquisition or joint venture using the sukuk proceeds at a price that adds EBITDA per share; a tariff revision that lifts reimbursement faster than input costs; and a free-float increase that broadens the institutional base. Any two of those together would justify revisiting the rating, because they would raise the growth path rather than the multiple.

Ownership is concentrated. Insiders hold a little under half the shares and the registry-compliant free float is a minority stake; the accounts describe no second controlling vehicle inside the group [S0][S4]. The exchange and the depository published a new high-shareholding-concentration screen in November 2026 that removes the names it captures from the IHSG calculation [S7]. The list is published as an image appendix and the archived article text does not reproduce the names, so we have not been able to verify whether Metro is on it; we make no claim about the group's index status in either direction [S7][S8]. The exchange is explicit that the screen is not a suspension, a delisting or a finding against a company [S7]. What the ownership data does establish is that the marginal buyer is retail and that a controlling holder has limited incentive to widen the float [S0][S4].

Related-party dealings are not a material channel here on the evidence we have. The revenue note states that there were no sales, service revenues or other revenues to related parties in FY2025 or FY2024 [S4]. Compensation to the board and commissioners is small relative to the cost base [S5]. The group's subsidiaries are almost entirely wholly owned, with minority interests of a rounding size on the consolidated balance sheet [S0]. That is a cleaner related-party picture than most small-cap Indonesian groups, and we credit it.

The capital structure is the governance issue that matters most to an equity holder. The group raised a trillion rupiah of sukuk in 2026, repaid half, and held the remainder in cash while paying financial expenses that consume nearly all of operating profit [S5]. A controlling shareholder with a large stake and a small float has less incentive to explain a refinancing to the market than a widely held company does, and the interim accounts give no use-of-proceeds note. We treat this as an optics-class flag: disclosed, legal, and value-relevant, but not evidence of extraction.

The dividend record is empty. The company has not paid a dividend since listing and the pack shows no distribution through FY2025 [S0]. With retained losses and a live capital programme, that is defensible; it also means the entire return to an equity holder at today's price depends on capital appreciation, which is exactly what our valuation says is unavailable.

On ESG, the company's own reporting covers patient safety and satisfaction, occupational health, waste and effluent management, and local employment. It reports a patient satisfaction score in the high nineties, a workforce that is entirely local, and effluent within regulatory standards with no sanctions or community complaints [S6]. These are self-reported and unaudited in the annual report, but they are specific and checkable. The material ESG risk for a hospital operator is clinical governance — infection control, medical error, licensing — and the accounts give no adverse event disclosure. We do not treat ESG as a valuation driver for this name; it is a licence-to-operate check that the company passes on the evidence available.

The next hard data point is the FY2026 audited result in the first quarter of 2027. It matters more than usual because it will show, for the first time, a full year of the new revenue base with an audited cost breakdown. We will be watching three lines: hospital services revenue against the nine-month run-rate; the claim-tariff difference as a percentage of hospital revenue; and operating expenses against revenue, because the 2026 result depended on that ratio falling. The nine-month comparatives for both lines are already in the interim accounts [S5].

The second catalyst is the sukuk. Half of the trillion rupiah issued in 2026 was repaid inside the same nine months, which suggests a maturity schedule that will require action within twelve months of the year-end accounts [S5]. The refinancing rate, and whether the group draws on its cash balance instead, will tell us whether the capital structure is being managed for equity holders or for liquidity.

The third is the float. A placing that widens the shareholder base would broaden the investor pool and, in our view, remove part of the price anomaly; the exchange reviews and republishes its concentration screens periodically [S7]. We would treat a large discounted placement as a negative for per-share value even as it improves liquidity, so the terms matter more than the event.

The fourth is the hospital under construction. The 367 IDR bn of advances outstanding has to become beds. When it does, the depreciation charge rises before the revenue does, and the first two quarters after opening will show whether the new capacity earns its cost of capital [S5].

Between reports we monitor the monthly registry data on foreign and institutional flows, the quarterly accounts for the claim-tariff line, and any disclosure of the use of the sukuk proceeds. The registry extract in the data pack is our source for float and price, and the interim accounts for the cost lines [S0][S5]. We will revise on any of the signposts set out above, and we will revisit the rating if hospital revenue growth holds at the 2026 rate for two more quarters with the cost ratio intact.

Hospital operators in this market are valued by investors on a small number of familiar metrics: enterprise value to EBITDA for the operating business, price to earnings once interest and depreciation are stable, and bed-count-based replacement cost for the asset base. Each fails at a different point in the cycle — EBITDA ignores the capex that creates the beds, earnings ignore the leverage that funds them, and replacement cost ignores the licence and the catchment. A valuation that uses all three, weighted toward the cash flow, is the minimum discipline for a company whose asset base is growing faster than its revenue.

bear.narrative: The 2026 revenue step-up proves to be a tariff/claim-settlement effect rather than a durable volume gain: hospital growth decelerates to 10% from FY2027E (6pp below base), the BPJS claim-tariff shortfall that already trebled to 82.22 in 9M-2026 keeps pressing gross margin 2pp lower, and the 370-day Sukuk Ijarah Series A of 500 is refinanced at 200bp over the 7.75% it pays today while a discounted placement of 8% of the shares funds the next phase, diluting per-share value (S5). Probabilities are 25%: the claims line is visible in the accounts and the sukuk wall is dated, but volume growth of the observed size is not yet proven to persist.

bull.narrative: The 2026 step-up is the new hospitals maturing and KRIS-ready capacity filling: hospital revenue compounds 6pp faster than base, the claim-tariff headwind is absorbed by tariff revisions so gross margin runs 2pp higher, the Sukuk Ijarah Series A is refinanced at 200bp below today's 7.75% as the programme seasons, and the 366.86 of advances convert into beds at the 9M-2026 42% hospital gross margin with no further cost build (S5,S6). The sukuk-funded cash is deployed into the next hospital, which is what management has guided to. 25% probability: it needs the volume trend to hold for another two quarters.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is calendar 2026, not the LTM: nine-month revenue to Sep-2026 of 366.56 (hospital services 333.96 plus investment income 32.60) plus a Q4 built as Q4-2025 hospital revenue of 106.69 grown at the 9M-2026 hospital rate of 41.95% gives 485.41 of hospital revenue and 518.01 in total, 17.8% above FY2025A. Using the LTM of 571.05 would count Q4-2025, which carried 97.80 of investment income that the 9M-2026 comparative shows as nil (S5,S4). No further investment income is forecast beyond the 32.60 already earned, because the policy note defines it as interest plus realised and unrealised trading gains, not a portfolio yield (S4). FY2027E hospital revenue grows 16% off that base; the blended rate is 8.7% because the non-recurring investment income drops out. FY2028E-FY2030E step down to 13/11/9% on the seven-hospital base with 366.86 of advances for property and equipment already paid (S5,S6,S3); the terminal 5% is nominal GDP less a capacity haircut.

assumptions.label: Gross margin
assumptions.basis: Hospital gross margin is 42.25% in 9M-2026 (hospital revenue 333.96 less cost of revenue 192.86) against 51.90% in 9M-2025, when the comparative carried no investment income (S5). The whole 9.7pp fall is the claim-tariff difference: 82.22 in 9M-2026 against 23.24 a year earlier, 24.6% of hospital revenue versus 9.9% (S5). Ex that line, hospital cost of revenue fell from 38.2% of hospital revenue to 33.1%, which is why operating profit still doubled. We hold the last actual hospital ratio: cash cost of sales at 51.66% of hospital revenue plus depreciation at 5.23% of revenue in FY2026E, with depreciation fading as the base grows. FY2026E blended margin of 46.36% is higher than the hospital ratio only because 32.60 of zero-cost investment income is inside revenue; from FY2027E that income drops out and the blended margin is the hospital margin.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month operating expenses were 96.53 on revenue of 366.56, 26.3%, against 145.14 for FY2025A on a 9M-2025 figure of 88.80, which leaves a Q4-2025 charge of 56.34, 1.9x the nine-month quarterly run-rate (S5,S4). The spike sits in salaries and allowances: Q4-2025 38.78 against a 9M-2025 quarterly average of 17.96, while 9M-2026 salaries grew only 7.6% and headcount fell from 881 to 848 (S4,S5). We treat it as a year-end compensation true-up tied to the restructuring and do not carry it into the forecast; carrying the LTM ratio would understate FY2026E EBITDA by about 26. FY2026E therefore builds opex as 96.53 plus a Q4 at the 9M-2026 quarterly run-rate, 128.71 or 24.8% of revenue, and holds that ratio flat because the same hospital count carries the next leg of revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation is disclosed only inside cost of revenue: 26.33 in FY2025A and 20.32 in nine months to Sep-2026, so 27.10 for calendar 2026, 5.23% of the revenue we forecast (S4,S5). We fade the ratio to 4.4% by FY2030E as revenue grows on the existing asset base and the 366.86 of advances already paid (S5) is depreciated over a larger base. The data pack carries no D&A, so this line is taken from the LK notes.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2024A-FY2025A capex of 226.9 and 210.8 was dominated by advance payments for property and equipment (216.46 and 202.41) for a hospital under construction, not by maintenance (S4). Those advances are already paid (366.86 still outstanding at Sep-2026, S5) and nine-month 2026 cash capex was only 11.2 (S5), so FY2026E is 4% of revenue. We rebuild to 8% by FY2028E to fund the next phase of bed capacity, which is roughly 1.9x the D&A charge and consistent with a network still adding hospitals (S3,S6).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital is structurally negative: trade payables and accrued expenses exceed receivables plus inventory, with an operating NWC of -7.15 at Sep-2026 (S0). We hold the FY2025A level of -4.0% of revenue, which is the average of the last three years, rather than the more favourable 2026 print.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The statutory corporate rate is 22%; the reported effective rate has been higher (36% in FY2025A, 44% in 9M-2026) on small pre-tax bases and non-deductible items (S4,S5). We use 22% for the forecast, the marginal rate a profitable hospital group should pay once the loss carry-forward is used, and note that the recent effective rate is higher.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Financial expenses were 80.36 in FY2025A on opening debt of 944.5 and 74.83 in nine months to Sep-2026 on a debt stock that rose from 1,083.6 to 1,551.4 (S4,S5); bank term loans carry 9.25% (S4). We use 8.5%, close to the FY2025A realised rate, rather than the lower nine-month average that mixes in the new sukuk proceeds.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Financial income was 15.56 on opening cash of 470.7 in FY2025A, but that included a 5.50 promissory-note coupon that did not repeat (S4). In 9M-2026 financial income was 4.83, of which 3.61 bank interest and 1.21 time-deposit interest, on an average cash balance near 716 that included the Rp500bn of unspent sukuk proceeds; annualised that is about 0.9% (S5). The balance sheet note says the group keeps only operational cash and the LK records 900.16 of cash at bank plus 61.50 in time deposits, so we cut the yield to the realised rate: 0.9% on the model's opening cash, which books about 4.2 in FY2026E and then applies to the larger 2027 cash balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the actual nine-month financing flow: Rp1,000bn of Sukuk Ijarah raised and Rp500bn of Sukuk Wakalah Series A repaid, so interest-bearing debt at Sep-2026 is 1,551.4 against 1,083.6 at Dec-2025 and the model's opening debt plus 467.7 reconciles to the LK total (S5). No further net borrowing is forecast: cash of 961.7 against 1,551.4 of debt covers the base-case capex. The balance-sheet lines then roll from the LK actual to the FY2026E year-end through our Q4 cash flow, which is why the model line and the September bridge net debt differ by that quarter's cash generation.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: other income was 2.86 in FY2025A and 0.74 in 9M-2026 (S4,S5), too small and too irregular to forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are 2.15 of a 3,026.2 equity at Sep-2026 (S0); we use 1% of net profit as in the last three years.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company has not paid a dividend since its 2020 IPO and carries a retained-loss position; a payout would require both profit and board approval (S4 notes no dividend; the pack shows zero DPS through FY2025A, S0).

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: 33,250m shares outstanding, no rights issue or buyback disclosed in the 2024 annual report or the 2026 interim accounts (S4,S5,S6).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House macro deck has real GDP at 5.3% and CPI at 3.3%, so long-run nominal GDP is about 8.6%; a mature seven-hospital network with bed capacity bounded by local catchment grows below that. We use 5%, a 3.6pp discount, which is also below the 9% final explicit year.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of 570.8 is the LTM, which includes Q4-2025 revenue of 204.5 of which 97.8 was investment income; 9M-2025 investment income was nil (S5 page 64). FY2026E gross margin of 47.4% is the 9M-2026 blend, where investment income is 32.6 of 366.6, or 8.9%. Applied to the LTM, 47.4% implies hospital-only gross profit of 140.1 on hospital revenue of 440.7, a 31.8% hospital margin against 42.2% actual. The revenue head and the margin come from different periods and cannot both stand.
challenges.answer: FY2026E rebuilt as calendar 2026: nine-month actual of 366.6 including 32.6 of investment income plus a Q4-2026 built from Q4-2025 hospital revenue grown at the 9M hospital rate, giving revenue 518.0 and a 46.4% blended margin. The LTM is discarded as a forward base because Q4-2025 carried 97.8 of investment income the 9M-2025 comparative shows as nil. Investment income is treated as a non-recurring line that stops after 2026, and §3 states revenue and margin come from the same period [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: The HSC and index claim is unsupported. S7 (detik, 383 HSC names) and S8 (kompas, 300 HSC names) contain no occurrence of CARE or Metro Healthcare; the lists are published as images. Neither article mentions LQ45, IDX30 or IDX80, yet the report asserts removal from all three in the summary and sections 1, 6 and 7.
challenges.answer: The HSC membership, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 removal and the no-passive-bid argument are deleted from the summary, §5, §6 and §7. §6 now cites only what S7 verifies — that BEI and KSEI published a 383-name HSC list effective 13 November 2026 removing captured names from the IHSG calculation — and states explicitly that the list is an image appendix we could not check against Metro, so we make no index claim either way [S7][S8].

challenges.challenge: The report reads hospital gross margin as rising from 34.3% in FY2025 to 42.2% in 9M-2026. The like-for-like comparison is 51.9% in 9M-2025 (revenue 235.3, cost of revenue 113.2, no investment income) to 42.2% in 9M-2026: a 9.7pp fall, not a rise. The forecast then holds the 9M-2026 blended margin flat.
challenges.answer: §3 now states the annual comparison misleads and gives the like-for-like nine-month comparison: the hospital gross margin fell several points year on year, and the whole of the fall is the claim-tariff difference, which rose from 34.96 in 9M-2025 to 82.22 in 9M-2026, a quarter of hospital revenue, while every other cost line grew at about half the rate of hospital revenue. The forecast holds the observed 9M-2026 hospital margin rather than assuming recovery, and the bull case is the settlement-true-up reading [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: Both cross-checks capitalise FY2025 one-off income. EV/EBITDA uses metric 96.34, of which 97.8 is investment income, so hospital EBITDA excluding it is negative; P/E uses np_parent of 5.15, also almost entirely investment income, at the forward peer median of 19.82x. The DCF meanwhile runs on FY2026E EBITDA of 146.1. The -46% and -89% divergences the engine flags are never explained.
challenges.answer: Corrected on QC - the engine strikes both multiples on trailing FY2025A metrics, not FY2026E. The trailing EV/EBITDA gives Rp29 a share against the DCF Rp32 because the multiple capitalises the one-off investment income while the valuation bridge deducts the investment book, so the effects broadly offset; the P/E on trailing parent profit gives Rp3 and is disclosed at a 10% weight rather than averaged in. Weights are 60/30/10 in assumptions and section 4 now states the trailing basis explicitly [S5][S4][S0].

challenges.challenge: The DCF is not tested against asset value. EV of 1,529.6 is 0.47x net PP&E of 3,263.1 at Sep-2026, and the implied exit is 8.9x FY2035 EBITDA against the 11.4x peer median the report itself uses. No replacement-cost, P/B or exit-multiple cross-check appears.
challenges.answer: §4 now carries the asset test: FY2026E net PP&E of 3,652.8 against a DCF enterprise value of 1,290.1, and a target below book value per share of 91.4. The paragraph reconciles the gap through return on capital — a mid-single-digit return on that asset base against an 11.0% WACC — states that replacement cost only sets a floor for an entrant earning its cost of capital, and states the implied exit multiple as a share of terminal value on FY2035E EBITDA, below the entry multiple the market pays today [S5][S0].

challenges.challenge: The 366.86 of advance payments for property and equipment (S5, F20) is cash already spent on beds that produce no revenue yet. It gets no bridge item and no explicit revenue line; the base case simply grows revenue 16/13/11/9% off the existing base. The house card says development assets are worth at least their sunk capex.
challenges.answer: The 366.864 of advances for property and equipment now sits in valuation.bridge at sunk cost with F20 and S5 as its evidence, probability one, worth about Rp11 a share. §4 states that the bridge credits cash already spent and the DCF earns only on assets operating today, so the advances are neither zeroed nor double-counted with future revenue from the beds they fund [S5].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E opex of 151.3 holds the LTM ratio of 26.5%. The LTM opex contains a Q4-2025 charge of 56.3 (FY2025 145.1 less 9M-2025 88.8), 1.9x the 29.6 quarterly run-rate, with no disclosed cause; 9M-2026 opex was 96.5, up 8.7% year on year. Carrying that spike into FY2026E understates EBITDA by about 26 if it was a year-end true-up.
challenges.answer: The Q4-2025 spike is identified from the notes as a salaries and allowances true-up: FY2025 salaries of 115.3 against 67.5 in the nine months, while headcount fell, so it is a year-end compensation charge rather than a cost level. FY2026E opex is therefore built as the 96.5 of nine-month actual plus one quarter at that run-rate, holding 24.8% of revenue flat, and the spike is not carried forward [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks only revenue growth, gross margin and opex. It has no share-count shock although section 7 says a discounted placing to fix the float is likely, no refinancing shock although 500 of sukuk sits in current liabilities, and no KRIS standard-class shock to private-room revenue.
challenges.answer: The bear case now carries four shocks: revenue growth six points below base, gross margin two points lower, cost of debt 200bp higher as the 500 Sukuk Ijarah Series A is refinanced, and an 8% discounted placement funding the next phase. The bull mirrors revenue, margin and the refinancing rate the other way. Dilution is one-sided because the evidence is one-sided: the company has no buyback mandate or treasury authority, so a negative share change would be invented, and that justification is recorded in qc_justifications scenario.mirror [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: cash_yield of 3.3% is the FY2025 realised rate on opening cash of 470.7. In 9M-2026 financial income was 4.83 on average cash near 716, about 0.9% annualised, on a balance that now includes the 500 of sukuk proceeds. The model books roughly 32 of financial income a year against a realised run-rate near 6.
challenges.answer: The cash yield is cut from the FY2025 realised 3.3% to the 9M-2026 realised rate of 0.9%: financial income of 4.83 in the nine months, of which 3.61 bank interest and 1.21 time-deposit interest, on average cash near 716 that included the unspent sukuk proceeds. FY2026E interest income is therefore 4.2, not the roughly 32 the old yield produced, and the basis records the change [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: The report says the unlevered beta of 0.70 is the card's default for the industry. fund record contains no beta default; it pins the COE band at 11-13% for IDR. fund record records beta_source as company parameter. A 0.70 unlevered beta for a stock with this volatility and leverage is unsupported.
challenges.answer: The claim that 0.70 is a card default is removed. §4 and params_basis now say plainly that the coverage universe carries no regression for CARE or its closest listed peers, and that the unlevered beta of 0.77 is calibrated from the house IDR band rather than observed, with the sensitivity table showing that a higher cost of capital lowers the value further, so the call does not rest on the choice [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: COE of 10.99% and WACC of 10.57% are below the card's 11-13% IDR band. The report acknowledges this in one sentence and moves on, but the card requires the breach to be argued; the sensitivity table shows about a sixth of the DCF value at plus one point.
challenges.answer: The below-band cost of capital is gone: with the unlevered beta at 0.77 the levered beta is 0.85, the cost of equity is 11.5% and the WACC 11.0%, at the floor of the eleven to thirteen per cent IDR band rather than under it. §4 states the beta is calibrated to that floor and that publishing an out-of-band rate for a leveraged, capital-intensive small cap was the wrong starting point [S0].

challenges.challenge: The balance-sheet paragraph is stale. It says gross debt was 1,083.6 at FY2025 and rose to 1,083.6 by September 2026, and that cash was 513.3. S5 shows interest-bearing debt of about 1,551.4 and cash of 961.7 at Sep-2026; 513.9 is the December 2025 total current assets, not cash. The valuation uses the right figures, the prose does not.
challenges.answer: The balance-sheet paragraph is restated from the September LK: interest-bearing debt of 1,083.6 at FY2025 rising to 1,551.4 at Sep-2026 after the Ijarah issue and Wakalah repayment, cash of 900.16 plus 61.50 in time deposits, and the 513.9 confusion removed. The paragraph explains that the model line shows 585.0 of year-end net debt because it rolls the September actual through Q4 cash flow, while the bridge uses September net debt of 589.7, the difference being that quarter [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: The report says 0.6% of DCF value is in the terminal period and defends that share. fund record gives tv_share of 0.602257, so it is 60.2%. The paragraph defends a number a hundred times too small.
challenges.answer: The 0.6% sentence is deleted. The paragraph now uses the engine placeholder, which resolves to 58.6% of value in the terminal period, and argues that weight properly: a ten-year explicit period fully charged for capex and working capital, terminal growth of 5% below nominal GDP, and an implied exit multiple below the entry multiple the market pays for FY2026E EBITDA today [S0].

challenges.challenge: The summary says the DCF is weighted at 0.6%, the EBITDA multiple at 0.3% and earnings at 0.1%, then says this produces Rp27. The configured weights are 60, 30 and 10.
challenges.answer: Corrected the summary weights from percentages of the target (0.6/0.3/0.1) to argument weights: the DCF now carries 60%, the EV/EBITDA cross-check 30% and P/E 10%, and the engine target moves accordingly.

missing_bull_case.note: No bull case is built on the model's own numbers: implied exit is 8.9x FY2035 EBITDA against the 11.4x peer median the report uses, and EV of 1,529.6 is 0.47x net PP&E of 3,263.1 with no replacement-cost or asset-floor cross-check. The 366.86 of prepaid beds is valued at zero.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear case shocks only growth, gross margin and opex. It has no share-count shock although section 7 says a discounted placing to fix the float is likely, no sukuk refinancing shock although 500 of sukuk sits in current liabilities, and no KRIS standard-class shock to private-room revenue.

assumption_realism.note: Anchor year is a period mismatch (C1); hospital gross margin actually fell 9.7pp like-for-like, from 51.9% in 9M-2025 to 42.2% in 9M-2026, not rose; FY2026E opex embeds a 56.3 Q4-2025 quarter at 1.9x the run-rate; tax is 22% against 36-43% actually paid.

evidence_and_citations.note: Credit where due: investment income inside revenue is correctly traced to S4 page 76 and S5 page 64, and the 7-hospital, 848-employee and 33.25bn-share facts all check out. But neither S7 nor S8 names CARE or Metro Healthcare, and the beta card default does not exist in the card.

valuation_method_fit.note: Terminal value is 60.2% of EV, not the 0.6% the report states; no implied-exit or multiple-survival test although modelled ROE is 1-3% through FY2035E against COE 11%; cross-checks capitalise FY2025 one-off earnings and the -46% and -89% divergences are unexplained.

bias_and_tone.note: The line that two cross-checks point lower still overstates support: on forward-consistent metrics they are about Rp32 and Rp20, at or above the DCF. The rating itself does survive doubling the bear probability, which moves the target to about Rp18, so the conclusion is sound even though the prose is not.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE of 10.99% and WACC of 10.57% sit below the compounder card's 11-13% IDR band and the report calls this just below without the argument the card requires. Peers are quoted on FY0 multiples while CARE's own drivers are FY1.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: implied FY2026E hospital gross margin of 31.8% against 42.2% actual; 366.86 of prepaid beds at zero; the Q4-2025 opex spike carried forward; EV below book PP&E with no impairment argument. Unjustified optimism: tax at 22% against 36-43% paid, and cash yield of 3.3% against 0.9% realised.

calibration.note: The FY2025A margin of 21.9% against a model 25.6%, a 3.69pp gap, has no qc_justifications entry; the 9M-2026 print supports it but the gate needs the source stated. Both BLOCK flags are justified and cite real filings.

signoff.notes: SELL is robust and internally coherent: DCF Rp32 vs price Rp356, EV/EBITDA Rp29 corroborates it, only the 10%-weighted P/E leg (Rp3) is unrepresentative and that is disclosed; the asset test (net PP&E 3,653 vs DCF EV 1,290) and the exit-multiple/entry-multiple argument are in section 4; the COE-out-of-band point is argued explicitly; FY2026E is rebuilt as calendar 2026, not the LTM. Remaining QC FIX/NOTE (Q9 Q4 salary true-up, Q10 give the exit multiple as a number, Q11 investment-income characterisation, Q13 earnings-quality output) do not move the -90.5% call - carry them into the next refresh.

bias.note: Both directions carry departures from the last actual and they broadly offset. Conservative: investment income of 32.60 already booked in 9M-2026 (S5 page 64) is included in FY2026E and then zeroed from FY2027E, worth roughly Rp9 a share on 32-43 of zero-cost revenue a year, and the 366.86 of paid-for advances get no revenue in the DCF. Optimistic: FY2026E opex of 128.7 carries no Q4 salaries true-up (worth about 15 of EBITDA, see Q9) and the tax rate is 22% against the 36% and 44% effective rates the LK shows. Neither set moves the target beyond Rp3-9 on a Rp34 target, and the -90.5% call does not depend on any of them: the reverse DCF needs 38.8% FY2027 revenue growth against the 8.7% base. Scenarios are mirrored on revenue growth, gross margin and cost of debt at 6pp, 2pp and 200bp, the bull premium (+62%) is larger than the bear discount (-37%), and base carries 50%. No stacked-bear pattern.

findings.finding: FY2026E opex of 128.7 contains no Q4 salaries true-up: 9M-2026 opex is 96.53 (S5) and the model implies a Q4 charge of 32.20, exactly the nine-month quarterly average, against a Q4-2025 charge of 56.34. The same intra-year accrual pattern repeats in both years, which is evidence the year-end catch-up recurs rather than being a one-off: 9M-2025 salaries of 53.88 are 62.7% of the FY2024 year of 85.98, and 9M-2026 salaries of 57.97 are 62.6% of the FY2025 year of 92.66 (S4 page 77, S5). The model therefore implies Q4-2026 salaries of about 24 against 38.78 actually booked in Q4-2025. Holding Q4-2026 salaries flat year on year costs about 15 of EBITDA, 11% of FY2026E, and about Rp2-3 per share. Raised as Q7 last round and left unanswered.

Section 4 asserts the multiple-survival test instead of showing it: the implied exit multiple is never printed. On the model own numbers the terminal value of 1,964.7 over FY2035E EBITDA of 230.8 is an 8.5x exit, against 89.7x entry on FY2026E EBITDA and the 12.4x peer median the report uses. Nor is the growth path reconciled to reinvestment: capex falls to 8% of revenue while D&A runs about 4.4%, so net investment is roughly 3.6% of revenue and the 8.7-13% growth years imply a very high incremental return with no ROIIC stated. The compounder card requires reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year and the numeric exit multiple.

The extreme_call justification calls the investment income non-recurring and cites the S4 accounting policy note, but that note only defines the line as interest on investment placements plus realised and unrealised trading gains; it says nothing about recurrence, and the LK shows 32.60 booked in 9M-2026 after 97.80 in Q4-2025. Zeroing it from FY2027E is a defensible modelling choice, but it is a choice worth about Rp9 a share and section 4 must present it as one, with its size, not as a sourced fact. Not a BLOCK: the -90.5% call does not depend on it.

Section 4 says debt costs 9.4% before tax, the realised rate across the sukuk and bank facilities. The rates the LK shows are 7.75% on the Sukuk Ijarah Phase I, 8.25% on Wakalah Series A and 9.25% on bank term loans, a blend near 8.1%, and the profit and loss model itself uses 8.5%. The engine figure of 9.45% is a WACC input rather than a realised rate; the WACC effect of the difference is about 5bp, so the band check is unaffected.

The earnings-quality card output is not in the report: no three-year accruals or cash-conversion line and no statement of IDX board or notation status. FY2025 net operating cash flow of 45.89 on net profit of 5.15, and 105.28 before interest and tax against the FY2024 negative 113.01, passes cleanly, which is worth saying because the thesis turns on whether the 2026 profit is real. A special-monitoring-board or notation letter would gate the call outright on a name at 3.9x book.

FY2026E hospital revenue of 485.4 puts Q4-2026 at 151.5, which is 42% above Q4-2025 of 106.69 and 36% above the 9M-2026 hospital quarterly average of 111.3. The seasonality is imported from Q4-2025, a quarter that also carried the 97.8 investment income and the 56.3 opex spike, and no alternative is shown. A flat Q4-2026 costs about 45 of revenue and 12 of EBITDA.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +4.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex is 4.0% of revenue in FY2026E because the heavy spend is already sunk: 202.41 of advance payments for property and equipment in FY2025A (216.46 in FY2024A) and 366.86 of those advances still outstanding at Sep-2026, with only 11.2 of cash capex in nine months of 2026 [S4][S5]. The +4.0pp to 8% from FY2027E rebuilds a normal build cycle at about 1.9x the D&A charge [S5][S6]; holding 4% to FY2035E would assume a seven-hospital network never adds another bed, which the outstanding advances and the annual report build-out plan contradict.

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only ['a.share_change'], bull only [])
flags.justification: The bear carries a dilution shock and the bull does not because share issuance is one-sided in the evidence: the company has an unissued Rp1.0tn of its Rp2.0tn Sukuk Ijarah programme with no buyback mandate or treasury authority disclosed anywhere in the FY2025 accounts or the 9M-2026 LK, so a negative share change would be invented rather than mirrored [S5][S4]. The refinancing shock is mirrored at 200bp each way, anchored on the 7.75% Series A coupon the company actually pays [S5]. The revenue and margin shocks stay mirrored at 6pp and 2pp.

flags.message: expected return -91%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The wide discount is produced by sourced inputs, not by a bearish haircut. FY2026E is calendar 2026, not the LTM: revenue of 518.0 includes the 32.60 of investment income already earned and excludes the 97.80 of Q4-2025 investment income the 9M comparative shows as nil [S5][S4]. On that revenue and a 46.4% blended margin the business earns about 138.5 of EBITDA against an 11,837 market capitalisation, so the price is about 85x 2026E EBITDA. From FY2027E the non-recurring investment income drops out [S4 policy note], capex rebuilds to 8% of revenue, and terminal free cash flow stays near 5% of invested capital. The reverse DCF shows what the price needs: FY2027E revenue growth far above our 8.7% blended rate, i.e. the 2026 step-up repeating every year with no fade and the investment income recurring [S0].
